alt: Candidates read one or two texts of about 400 to 450 words, use, develop and evaluate their ideas, and write about 250 to 350 words as a speech, email, report, letter or article. The one compulsory question carries 25 marks: 15 for writing (W1 to W5) and 10 for reading (R3 and R5).
caption: Read, work on the ideas, write in the set form: 15 marks for writing, 10 for reading.

alt: Three steps of rising height: use (take relevant ideas, the minimum), develop (consequences, fresh examples, connections, applying ideas to the audience) and evaluate (judge evidence, bias, strength and gaps). An example shows a road’s shorter journey times developed into more sleep for students.
caption: Using the sources is the minimum; high reading marks come from developing and evaluating them.

alt: Six questions for judging a source: fact or opinion, whose perspective, bias, evidence, conflict between sources and gaps, each with what to look for. An example sentence questions a developer’s unsupported claim and its neutrality.
caption: Turn the syllabus words into questions and ask them of every source.

after: ## The five forms and their conventions
alt: A grid of the five forms (speech, email, report, letter, article) showing how each opens, how it is shaped and what register it uses, from a speech that addresses its audience directly to an impersonal, objective report. W4, register, is assessed in directed writing.
caption: The form and audience in the question decide the opening, the shape and the register.

alt: Three purposes compared: discursive writing weighs both sides and reaches a judgement, argumentative writing defends a position with reasons and answers counter-arguments, and persuasive writing moves the audience to agree or act. Each shows a cue word from a question.
caption: The question’s wording tells you whether to weigh, argue or persuade.

alt: Five planning steps: read the question for form, audience, purpose and bullet points; read the sources twice, marking U for useful points, D for points to develop and E for points needing evaluation; decide a position; plan four or five paragraphs; plan the opening and closing.
caption: Annotate the sources U, D and E so every paragraph has something to develop or judge.

alt: Points from a council leaflet and a shopkeeper’s letter feed a letter to the council. The model paragraph uses the safety point, evaluates the vague claim that schemes were “popular” and the shopkeeper’s complaint, then develops a consequence and a solution: consult traders and trial alternate Saturdays.
caption: Development grows from the sources’ conflict, which is what makes it development rather than invention.
